title: Throughput harmonization: continuous batching, max_num_seqs & token ceilings
summary: Deep technical session on tuning Redwood runtime for ArgonWave's peaky LLM inference. Focus on continuous batching parameters, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, token ceilings), KV cache warmup patterns, and quantization tradeoffs for on-prem VPC deployment. Action items: run controlled benchmarks with max_num_seqs sweep, share quant profiles, provide suggested scheduler config and sample load generator script.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-02 16:00 UTC
Duration: 41 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood PM); Jordan (CTO - ArgonWave), Priya (ML Infra), Marcus (SRE), Alex (Backend)

Auto-summary: quick recap of current infra (ArgonWave running internal transformer-based summarization service on 4x A100s), goal to push throughput on on-prem racks while keeping 95th latency under 250ms. Explore continuous batching parameters, max_num_seqs caps, token ceilings, KV cache prewarm and quantization impact.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for making time today, i know we booked extra to get into the weeds on tuning, so Ethan will start with a quick runtime recap then we'll get into your metrics and knobs.
[00:20] Ethan: cool thanks Maya, hi all. Just to set context, Redwood's continuous batcher tries to group inflight sequences into multi-sequence batches up to max_num_seqs and then issues a single forward. The knobs that most affect throughput/latency are max_num_seqs, token ceiling per request, max_tokens_per_batch and the slot window timeout.
[00:45] Jordan: uh-huh, and our main pain is spikes...we see big bursts during ingest windows which saturate the GPU and latency spikes to 600ms sometimes. We're on-prem, VPC isolated, so can't just spill to hosted.
[01:10] Priya: quick detail — our typical request lengths are 12-80 tokens, median 28, with some outliers at 300 tokens for long docs.
[01:30] Ethan: that distribution matters a lot. If you let max_num_seqs be high, shorter seqs pack well and throughput increases; but long outliers cause large per‑batch time and the 95th goes up.
[01:52] Marcus: can you define "max_num_seqs" again? we see both max_num_seq and max_num_seqs in configs and it's confusing in our YAML.
[02:08] Ethan: yeah sorry, slight naming drift across releases — in Redwood 1.8 it's max_num_seqs (plural) — it's the per‑GPU sequence packing cap. If it's 64 you'll never pack more than 64 sequences per forward even if there are slots.
[02:28] Alex: what about token ceilings? we've tried a token_limit of 512 but i think that just drops requests.
[02:40] Ethan: token ceilings act as per‑request truncation when a single request exceeds the limit; it's a safety knob to prevent huge variance. There's also max_tokens_per_batch which caps the total tokens in a pack — that's really useful to avoid one long sequence blocking many short ones.
[03:05] Jordan: so in practice if we set max_num_seqs=96 and max_tokens_per_batch=8192 do we get better steady throughput? we measured earlier ~14k tokens/s but that was with cold KV hit rate.
[03:26] Ethan: in ideal steady warm-cache you'd likely see 20–28k tokens/s on A10048 depending on quant. But with cold KV cache you'll see big variance. Our recommendation is to tune three levers: reduce max_num_seqs to keep tail small, set max_tokens_per_batch to protect against long outliers, and adjust the slot timeout to balance packing vs latency.
[03:50] Priya: slot timeout — that's the time the batcher waits for more sequences before sending a partial batch?
[03:58] Ethan: exactly. If you set timeout too long you lower latency percentiles but increase average latency; too short and you lose throughput. For your bursty load we usually start at 20ms then tune up to 60ms to increase pack depth.
[04:20] Marcus: ok, about KV cache — we've noticed first requests after deploy are much slower, what are best practices for prewarm?
[04:34] Ethan: KV warm is a thorny one on on‑prem. You have a few options: run a synthetic prewarm generator that sends representative prefixes to populate KV and local caches, use a stale-cache warmup after deploy, or pin hot routes to minimize eviction. Note that eviction policy and per‑GPU KV capacity are configurable but on-prem racks with limited CPU mem require careful sizing.
[04:58] Jordan: do you persist the KV cache across inference workers or is it local RAM per process?
[05:05] Ethan: currently per worker process; with dedicated pools we can keep processes warm longer and reduce churn. For Private on‑prem we provide tooling to serialize and rehydrate KV across restarts but you have to enable it in the config.
[05:25] Alex: you mentioned quant earlier — we tried Q8 and saw a 12% drop in quality for our summarization task, is that typical?
[05:38] Ethan: quant impacts are model and task specific. int8 often gives good perf/cost wins with minimal quality loss for generation, int4 can be more brittle. We recommend running evals against your eval set — Redwood Optimize can produce quant profiles that highlight tokens where logits deviate. For summarization int8 is usually safe but watch hallucination delta.
[06:05] Priya: is the quantization applied at runtime or compiled into kernel? we run an optimized kernel on our on‑prem setup.
[06:14] Ethan: both — we ship quantized runtime paths. For some backends we JIT a quant kernel at load and choose the best path at compile time. There are also per‑layer quant profiles if you need mixed precision.
[06:34] Jordan: let's go through a concrete tuning plan — what sweep should we run first?
[06:41] Ethan: my suggested plan: baseline run with current config, then three sweeps: (A) max_num_seqs at [32,64,96], (B) max_tokens_per_batch at [4096,8192,16384], (C) slot timeout at [20ms,40ms,80ms]. Keep quant constant for the first set. Track tokens/s, 50/95/99 latency, KV hitrate and GPU util.
[07:10] Marcus: what about token ceilings per request to protect from 300‑token outliers?
[07:18] Ethan: set per_request_token_limit to something like 256 or 512 depending on SLAs; for lens that must be long you can route those to a separate pool with higher max_tokens_per_batch or lower packing to avoid affecting short‑seq routing.
[07:39] Priya: we have multi‑tenant traffic — how do we avoid one tenant hogging the pack slots?
[07:47] Ethan: Redwood supports priority windows and token budgets per route. Low priority requests can be placed in separate queues or given lower slot priority. There's also adaptive throttling to enforce per‑tenant token ceilings.
[08:05] Jordan: in terms of throughput numbers — can you give a ballpark for our hardware? we're 4x A100 40GB.
[08:14] Ethan: ballpark per GPU in warm KV, int8: 18–25k tokens/s depending on seq length distribution. With cold KV that can drop by 30–60% until hitrate stabilizes. So cluster wide multiply by 4 but you need to account for multi‑process concurrency overhead.
[08:38] Alex: our ops concern is network — VPC NAT egress constraints increase tail. any config to mitigate?
[08:47] Ethan: yes, reduce external calls in the hot path, use local model assets (no round trips), and increase connection pooling. For VPC private deployments, ensure your control plane and metrics streams are on a high‑priority path and consider colocating model-serving on same subnet to reduce hop count.
[09:09] Priya: about eviction, you mentioned pinning hot routes — what's the memory cost?
[09:18] Ethan: pinning keeps KV entries resident, so memory increases linearly with pinned KV size. We recommend pinning just prefixes that are extremely high volume; everything else uses LRU. We'll share a small script that computes candidate prefixes by request frequency.
[09:34] Maya: Jordan, can you tell us the typical QPS distribution across the day — is it peaky by minute or hour?
[09:44] Jordan: mostly minute‑level bursts during ingest windows — 2–3 minute spikes every 15 minutes when workers flush. Peak QPS reaches 4500 briefly.
[09:58] Ethan: ok then slot timeout at 40–60ms and moderate max_num_seqs (64) is a good starting point to smooth bursts while keeping tail reasonable.
[10:12] Marcus: what about backpressure? when queue grows do you prefer token throttling or reject?
[10:20] Ethan: better to shed gracefully — token throttling with priority windows so critical traffic remains. Rejection should be rare except for overloaded maintenance windows.
[10:34] Priya: curious — any kernel-level knobs we should be aware of? tiling, flash attention params?
[10:43] Ethan: yes there are kernel knobs — tile sizes and attention kernel selection can be influenced by sequence length bins. Redwood runtime auto-selects but you can pin kernels per model if you have a stable distribution. We'll include recommended kernel hints for long‑tail workloads.
[11:05] Jordan: let's talk test harness — we need an example load generator that simulates our mix of 12–80 median and 300 token outliers.
[11:14] Ethan: we'll send a simple python/gRPC loadgen that replays traces, supports controlled KV warm patterns and toggles quant. It also emits KV hitrate metrics.
[11:26] Alex: do you instrument per‑batch composition? we want to see histograms of sequences per batch and token distribution.
[11:34] Ethan: yes Redwood exposes per‑batch histograms and sequencing heatmaps in the Console; we'll show you how to hook the tracing and export to your Datadog.
[11:48] Priya: a weird behavior we saw: when we increased max_num_seqs to 128 GPU util jumped but 95th latency also jumped and tail became worse than before. Why would util increase and tail worsen?
[12:02] Ethan: that's classic packing starving small latency buckets. High max_num_seqs lets batches accumulate many sequences including a few long ones — the long ones increase per forward compute time so small latency requests get stuck waiting for the big batch to finish. It's the herd effect.
[12:23] Jordan: so solution is to cap max_num_seqs and use max_tokens_per_batch to prevent long ones from hogging. Also route long requests to a different pool.
[12:36] Ethan: exactly. Two pools pattern works well: pool A tuned for short latency‑sensitive requests (low max_num_seqs, small timeout), pool B for heavy long requests (higher packing, higher tokens per batch).
[12:52] Marcus: okay practical question: when we change these knobs do we need to restart workers?
[12:58] Ethan: most knobs are hot reloadable via config API, but some kernel-level or precompile quant paths require a restart. We'll mark which ones are safe and which require redeploy.
[13:12] Priya: about quant again — can we do mixed quant across layers to protect some attention blocks?
[13:21] Ethan: yes mixed quant is supported. Redwood Optimize can propose layer‑wise candidates. That often hits a sweet spot: int8 for most, keep int16 for sensitive layers.
[13:34] Jordan: curious about metrics to monitor in real time during your sweep.
[13:41] Ethan: monitor tokens/s, 50/95/99 lat, batch size distribution, KV hitrate, GPU util, GPU memory pressure, and per‑tenant token spend. Also track sequencing waits and queue depth.
[14:00] Alex: do you provide automated suggestions? like an optimizer that reads metrics and suggests knob changes?
[14:07] Ethan: Redwood Optimize gives suggestions and can auto‑propose batching profiles based on trace analysis. We don't recommend fully automatic changes for production without human oversight, but it can shortlist configs.
[14:20] Maya: note to team — we'll include Redwood Optimize output in follow up.
[14:26] Jordan: can you give an example config snippet for the two‑pool approach?
[14:32] Ethan: sure — (paraphrasing) pool A: max_num_seqs: 32, max_tokens_per_batch: 4096, slot_timeout_ms: 25; pool B: max_num_seqs: 128, max_tokens_per_batch: 32768, slot_timeout_ms: 100. Route by route rules: short prefix -> pool A, long route -> pool B. We'll attach YAML after the call.
[15:01] Priya: how do we measure KV hitrate over time? we've been seeing it oscillate after restarts.
[15:09] Ethan: use the per‑route KV hitrate metric we emit — look at warmup slope. If hitrate stabilizes within a minute you're good; if it takes >5 minutes you need sustained prewarm. Also check eviction metrics — frequent evictions mean capacity undersized.
[15:26] Marcus: anything we can do to reduce eviction frequency without adding memory?
[15:31] Ethan: tune eviction policy to LRU with size buckets; reduce pinning; use prefix aggregation to reduce unique keys. Often the best is trimming TTLs for low‑value entries so hot ones stay resident.
[15:48] Jordan: okay, let's talk about safety valves — token ceilings and request truncation — we need to avoid user visible truncation for some clients.
[15:58] Ethan: for those clients you can disable truncation and route them to a high‑capacity pool. For public routes use truncation as a blunt safety to protect global SLOs.
[16:10] Priya: we'll need RBAC to control who can change those knobs. Is that built in?
[16:16] Ethan: yes Console supports RBAC and audit logs; SSO/SAML integration is supported for Private. That's part of our enterprise package.
[16:26] Alex: we run a hybrid: some workloads in cloud and some on-prem. Any recommended network config?
[16:34] Ethan: keep hot inference in on‑prem, use cloud for batch evals, and ensure control plane traffic is over private links. Also make sure quant profiles are replicated across environments to avoid perf mismatch.
[16:51] Jordan: about benchmarks — we'll run the sweeps. What logs do you need from us?
[16:58] Ethan: send per‑batch histograms, trace spans for tail ops, KV hitrate series, and GPU metrics. Also the loadgen trace so we can replay.
[17:10] Maya: quick check — do you have any red flags for the 4x A100 setup?
[17:15] Ethan: mostly KV mem sizing and eviction tuning; also be mindful of NUMA layout if you run multiple processes per socket. We recommend 1 process per GPU with pinned CPU affinities when possible.
[17:31] Priya: interesting — NUMA effects have bitten us before. We'll look at process pinning.
[17:38] Alex: any tips for interpreting batch histograms? sometimes the average is fine but 99th is bad.
[17:45] Ethan: histogram tails often point to either long outliers in the pack or a cold KV miss. Correlate 99th spikes with batch size and KV hitrate at that time.
[17:58] Jordan: can Redwood console surface the correlation automatically?
[18:04] Ethan: yes we have correlation panels — we'll show you how to add a composite panel for batch size vs 95th latency and KV hitrate overlay.
[18:18] Priya: do we have to pay extra for longer metrics retention to run these analyses?
[18:24] Maya: retention is tiered — we'll include options in the commercial follow up.
[18:31] Marcus: one more deep question — when continuous batching groups many sequences the KV cache indexing can become a bottleneck — any guidance?
[18:40] Ethan: make sure KV lookup code is optimized for vectorized ops; we use contiguous memory layouts and batch lookups. If your backend does per-key RPCs you'll lose the benefit. Also watch CPU threads for KV lookups; sometimes adding a few threads for lookup parallelism helps.
[19:00] Jordan: ok let's move to action items recap.
[19:05] Maya: recap: Redwood will send: tuned scheduler YAML, sample loadgen, quant profile export, kernel hints, and a short runbook for KV prewarm. ArgonWave will run the 3 sweeps and upload logs. We'll schedule a follow up to review results.
[19:25] Priya: timeline sounds good. We'll aim to run benchmarks next week.
[19:29] Alex: one last question — for the long requests could we implement server side streaming to reduce per‑request max tokens?
[19:37] Ethan: yes streaming helps both latency and memory pressure; it's a good pattern for long outputs.
[19:43] Jordan: great thanks everyone.
[19:46] [end of meeting]

Notes on transcription: some product internals mis‑spelled (max_num_seq vs max_num_seqs), occasional mis‑recognitions like "K V cash" for KV cache, and quant sometimes transcribed as "Q8" or "Q eight".
